title: Phonology
goals: Learn the sound system of Cantonese: initial and final consonants, vowels and diphthongs, the six tones and colloquial tone change
Overview: Cantonese is named after the city of Canton (Guangzhou in Mandarin)
Overview: spoken in Guangdong, Guangxi, Hong Kong, Macau, oversea Chinese communities (Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia, Toronto, Vancouver, LA, SF, NY)
Overview: mistakenly regarded as a "dialect" of Chinese (especially in mainland China)
Overview: Mandarin grammar cannot be applied straightforwardly to Cantonese
Overview: Cantonese and Mandarin are as different as various Romance languages

grammar.title: Consonants: initials
grammar.summary: Cantonese initials fall into unaspirated, aspirated, fricative and nasal/liquid series; the unaspirated/aspirated pairs (b/p, d/t, g/k, gw/kw, z/c) are distinguished only by a burst of air.
grammar.body:
Initials table (Unaspirated / Aspirated / Fricative / Nasal-liquid):
Bilabial: b / p / f / m
Dental/alveolar: d / t / s / n, l
Velar/glottal: g / k / h / ng
Labio-velar: gw / kw
Alveolar affricates: z / c
- The fricatives and nasals are pronounced the same as in English
- The first two columns may post more difficulty because they are distinguished by aspiration - a burst of air (e.g., bat1 'pen', d- as in deoi3 'pair' and g- as in gwai3 'expensive')
- In the labio-velar consonants gw and kw, the initial velar consonant is articulated more or less simultaneously with the bilabial [w] (e.g., gwaa3 'hang' and kwan4 'skirt')

grammar.title: Consonants: the affricates z and c
grammar.summary: z and c are distinguished by aspiration; their exact sound depends on the following vowel (alveo-palatal before i, yu, eo/eoi; alveolar elsewhere).
grammar.body:
- [z] and [c] are distinguished by aspiration, pronunciation differed by following vowels
- (i) Before the front vowels i, yu and eo or eoi they are alveo-palatal, respectively, formed with the tongue touching both the alveolar ridge and the palate, the sounds are fairly close to their English counterparts as in 'June' and 'choose'
- (ii) In all other cases they are alveolar, [ts] and [ts'] respectively, formed at the front of the mouth (like d and t) at the alveolar ridge just behind the teeth

grammar.title: Semivowels w- and j-
grammar.summary: The semivowels w- and j- begin syllables and sound much as in English.
grammar.body: - The semivowels w- and j- also occur at the beginning of a syllable. They can be pronounced much the same as in English

grammar.title: Consonants: nasals (ng- and n/l)
grammar.summary: The velar nasal ng- can begin a syllable but is frequently dropped by speakers; words beginning with n- are mostly pronounced with l- instead.
grammar.body:
The velar nasal written as ng- is a single consonant which presents two problems:
1. It is basically the same sound in English words like 'sing' and 'singer', but in Cantonese it can begin a syllable, as in ngo5 'I/me' (can be produced by pronouncing 'singer' as 'si-nger')
2. Cantonese speakers frequently do not pronounce it where expected. Thus the pronoun 'I' is often heard as o5, 'duck' is either ngaap3 or aap3, while ng5 'five' may be pronounced as m5 instead.
Similar problem arises with the distinction between n and l, although certain words begin with n, notably the pronoun nei5 'you', most speakers pronounce these with l instead:

grammar.title: Syllabic nasals
grammar.summary: m and ng occur as syllables in their own right: m4 'not', ng5 'five', ng4 'Ng'.
grammar.body:
- The nasal consonants m and ng occur as syllables in their own right
- The most frequently encountered examples are:
- 唔 m4 not (the main negative word)
- 五 ng5 five (also pronounced m5)
- 吴 ng4 Ng (a common surname)

grammar.title: Consonants: finals
grammar.summary: Only the stops -p, -t, -k (unreleased) and the nasals -m, -n, -ng occur at the end of a syllable.
grammar.body:
Only two kinds of consonants occur at the end of a syllable
1. the stops -p, -t, -k (unreleased as in "yep" in English), more difficult to hear than produce:
   baat3 Eight vs. baak3 hundred
   sap1 ce1 wet car vs. sat1 ce1 Missing car vs. sak1 ce1 Traffic jam
2. The nasals -m, -n, -ng: these are easily pronounced:
   saam1 Three vs. saan1 To close vs. saang1 Alive
   naam4 South vs. naan4 Difficult vs. laang5 cold
Note don't pronounce -ng words with -n such as hok6 saang1 'student' for hok6 saan1

grammar.title: Vowels: eight in Cantonese
grammar.summary: Cantonese has eight vowels: a, aa, i, e, o, u, yu, eo.
grammar.body:
Vowel / Cantonese / Translation / English counterpart:
a - bat1 Pen - Similar to the vowel in "but"
aa - saam1 Three - Similar to the vowel in "father"
i - si1 Silk - Similar to the vowel in "see"
e - leng3 Pretty - Similar to the vowel in "pet"
o - do1 Many - Similar to the vowel in "paw"
u - fu3 Trousers - Similar to the vowel in "fool"
yu - syu1 Book - Similar to the vowel in French "tu"
eo - seon3 letter - Similar to the vowel in French "Peugeot"

grammar.title: Vowels: long and short a
grammar.summary: Minimal pairs distinguished only by vowel length (a vs aa).
grammar.body:
- The following minimal pairs differ in the length of the vowel:
sam1 heart / saam1 Three
man6 Ask / maan6 Slow
hang4 Permanent / haang4 Walk
kat1 Cough / kaa1 Card

grammar.title: Vowels: front rounded vowels yu and eo
grammar.summary: yu and eo are single vowels made at the front of the mouth with rounded lips (like French u / eu).
grammar.body:
- The digraphs yu and eo represent single vowels produced at the front of the mouth with rounded lips
- yu is similar to French 'u' and German 'ü'. In English something like it appears in the second syllable of 'issue'.
- eo is similar to French 'eu' as in the second syllable in 'hors d'oeuvre'. English speakers may try to pronounce 'her' with rounded lips (as if pouting)

grammar.title: Variable vowels
grammar.summary: High vowels become more open before the velar consonants -k and -ng.
grammar.body:
- The sound of a vowel can be affected by a following consonant. High vowels become more open before the velar consonants -k and -ng:
sik6 eat / sek6 Stone
ging1 Pass by / geng1 Be afraid
luk6 six / lok6 To go down
tung4 with / tong4 sugar
zeok3 wear / ceot1 Go out
coeng1 window / zeon1 Bottle

grammar.title: Vowels: diphthongs
grammar.summary: Diphthongs shift from one vowel to another within one syllable: iu, oi, ou, ei, ui, eoi.
grammar.body:
- These combinations of two vowel sounds are produced by shifting from one vowel to another over the course of one syllable:
iu - giu3 call(ed) - As in English 'few'
oi - coi3 Vegetable - As in English 'boy'
ou - dou3 Arrive - As in English 'hold'
ei - sei3 Four - As in English 'say'
ui - gui6 Tired - As in English 'goo-ey' (but pronounced as only one syllable)
eoi - seoi3 tax - The front rounded vowel eo followed by the glide i

examples.en: Tired (ui, as in 'goo-ey' in one syllable)
Tax (eoi: eo followed by the glide i)

grammar.title: Vowels: diphthongs with short a and long aa
grammar.summary: Diphthongs come in short-a (ai, au) and long-aa (aai, aau) versions; aai is like 'sky', aau like 'how'.
grammar.body:
- There are diphthongs corresponding to both short a and long aa, the long diphthongs are close to those in English: aai is similar to that in 'sky', aau to that in 'how'
ai: sai1 west / aai: saai1 to waste
ai: mai5 Uncooked rice / aai: maai5 to buy
au: gau3 enough / aau: gaau3 to teach
au: lau6 leak / aau: naau6 to scold

grammar.title: Tones: deviation in pitch changes the identity of a word
grammar.summary: The same syllable with a different tone is a different word.
grammar.body:
Deviation in pitch changes the identity of a word
High level / Low level / Mid level / Low level (column headings as printed on the slide):
san1 New / san6 kidney / gau3 enough / gau6 old, dated
syu1 book / syu6 tree / dim3 To touch / dim6 OK, done
lau1 jacket / lau4 apartment / ngo2 goose / ngo5 I
jat1 bun3 One half / jat1 bun2 One (book) / ci2 teeth / ci5 resemble

grammar.title: The six tones
grammar.summary: For beginners six tones are plenty (Hong Kong Cantonese): 1 high level, 2 high rising, 3 mid level, 4 low falling, 5 low rising, 6 low level.
grammar.body:
How many tones? Different dialects of Cantonese vary
- For beginner six tone are plenty (based on Hong Kong Cantonese) shown with vowel a as an example
Tone table (Rising / Level / Falling):
High: a2 rising (high to mid), a1 level
Mid: a3 level
Low: a5 rising (low to mid), a6 level, a4 falling
Pitch chart: 1 high level; 2 rises from low-mid to high; 3 mid level; 5 rises from low-mid to mid; 6 low-mid level; 4 falls from low-mid to low

grammar.title: Tones: useful strategies for beginners
grammar.summary: The three level tones are easiest; tone 1 is like 'see!', tone 6 like 'se' in 'select', tone 3 halfway; tone 4 has a creaky voice; English intonation approximates the rising and falling tones.
grammar.body:
- 3 level tones (high, mid, and low) are relatively easy to recognize and produce (in musical terms, the difference between the high and mid is 1.5 tones, and between mid and low is 1 whole tone)
- Tone 1 is similar to English "see!", tone 6 is similar to "se" in "select", tone 3 is halfway between tones 1 and 6.
- It is more demanding to distinguish between low level and low falling, but the low-falling tone (i.e. 4th) as in lai4 'come' can often be recognized by a 'creaky' voice quality as the pitch reaches the bottom of the speakers voice range (similar to "cy" in "fancy")
English intonation patterns approximate some of the tones:
- High-rising tone as in dim2 'how' resembles a question showing surprise
- Low-rising tone as in ngo5 'I' begins with slight dip and can be compared to a hesitant 'well...'
- Low falling tone as in jan4 'person' resembles a dismissive intonation as in a calm but definitive 'no'

grammar.title: Tone change (i): nouns at the end of a compound or phrase
grammar.summary: In colloquial speech the affected syllable takes a high rising tone (tone 2) instead of its usual low tone; this happens to nouns at the end of a compound or phrase.
grammar.body:
- Occurs in colloquial speech
- The affective syllable pronounced with a high rising tone (tone 2) instead of the usual low (level or falling) tone.
- (i) Nouns at the end of a compound or phrase:
jan4 Person but neoi5 jan2 woman
jyut6 month but co5 jyut2 Spend a month resting after giving birth
man4 hok6 literature but jing1 man2 English (language)
jyu4 daan2 fish-cake but tiu4 jyu2 a/the fish
lau4 tai1 staircase but deng2 lau2 Top floor, penthouse
jat1 hap6 syu1 A box of books but jat1 go3 hap2 A box
jat1 dip6 coi3 A dish of vegetables but jat1 zek3 dip2 A dish

examples.en: Spend a month resting after giving birth

grammar.title: Tone change (ii) and (iii): names with aa3-/lou5- and reduplicated adjectives
grammar.summary: Names with the prefix aa3- or lou5- and the second syllable of reduplicated adjectives also take the high rising changed tone.
grammar.body:
- (ii) Names with the prefix aa3- or lou5-:
can4 saang1 Mr. Chan but aa3 can2 Chan (colloquial)
lai4 saang1 Mr. Lai but lou5 lai2 Old (Mr) Lai
- (iii) Reduplicated adjectives, in which the second syllable changes to a high rising tone
so4 foolish but so4 so2 dei2 silly
fei4 fat but fei4 fei2 dei2 Chubby

notes.title: The Cantonese language
notes.body: Named after the city of Canton (Guangzhou in Mandarin). Spoken in Guangdong, Guangxi, Hong Kong, Macau and oversea Chinese communities (Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia, Toronto, Vancouver, LA, SF, NY). Mistakenly regarded as a "dialect" of Chinese (especially in mainland China). Mandarin grammar cannot be applied straightforwardly to Cantonese; Cantonese and Mandarin are as different as various Romance languages.

notes.title: How many tones?
notes.body: Different dialects of Cantonese vary. For beginners six tones are plenty (based on Hong Kong Cantonese). The slide's pitch chart shows tone 1 high level, tone 2 rising to high, tone 3 mid level, tone 5 rising to mid, tone 6 low-mid level and tone 4 falling to low.
